description: Two distinctly scoped Irish cultural and statutory records; source-backed narratives, not a claim of published long-form reviews.

records.headline: St Brigid’s Day: Ireland’s spring tradition
records.origin: The traditional date is 1 February, associated with Lá Fhéile Bríde and the older seasonal festival Imbolc. Ireland’s government describes Brigid’s cultural roots and connections with the return of spring.
records.why: The date is rooted in Irish seasonal and religious heritage, not a modern statutory institution in the same way as a public holiday.
records.whyThisDate: 1 February is the traditional feast and spring-season marker, distinct from the employment public holiday.
facts: Imbolc marks a traditional point in the seasonal calendar.
The Irish public holiday created from 2023 can occur on a different date.
The traditional day is not proof that every workplace has a public-holiday entitlement on 1 February.

records.headline: Why Ireland added a St Brigid’s public holiday
records.origin: The Irish government introduced a new annual public holiday from 2023 to coincide with the period around Imbolc and St Brigid’s Day. Ireland’s Workplace Relations Commission confirms the first-Monday-in-February rule with an exception when 1 February is Friday.
records.why: The new public holiday recognizes a culturally significant point in the Irish calendar. The inaugural cultural programme also highlighted and celebrated women’s contributions.
records.whyThisDate: The first Monday of February, unless Friday 1 February is the holiday; the choice connects with the traditional 1 February observance.
facts: The holiday first became permanent from 2023.
2026: Monday 2 February; 2027: Monday 1 February; 2028: Monday 7 February; 2029: Monday 5 February.
The Friday 1 February exception applies in 2030.
A public-holiday employment entitlement is not identical to a guaranteed day off for every worker.
